extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in history of technology, carpentry, and craftsmanship
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-science / magazine-style historical survey of the development of carpentry, its practices, institutions (guilds), and notable technical achievements across cultures and eras. Focus is descriptive and aimed at informed general readers rather than practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurors' inspection of wood and seal
rubrics_metrics.description: As the choice of materials was of paramount importance for the security of the community at large, it was the jurors' duty to examine all wood before it could be used; the use of wood upon which the jurors had not thought fit to put their seal entailed heavy fines and even the suspension of the transgressor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors (selected among masters) inspected and approved wood before use; unapproved wood carried severe penalties. Purchases made in advance could be rejected if jurors found the wood unsatisfactory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution rule to prevent monopoly / prioritize public utility
rubrics_metrics.description: On the arrival of the merchandise, the purchaser could not take possession of the whole cargo, if his brother-tradesmen were not provided with sufficient materials to go on with work in hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision prevented monopoly and placed public utility above personal interest; it allowed jurors to withhold approval and thus stop a single buyer from monopolizing supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship duration and early obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The apprenticeship lasted four years, in the first of which the apprentice was forced to pay his master from one to three farthings per diem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apprenticeship was a formal multi-year period with economic obligations; training combined practical work and payment to the master, reflecting structured entry into the craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work-hours and night-work restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the statutes of the Paris brotherhood, carpenters were bound not to work from nine o'clock on Saturday night till Monday morning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Night work was restricted; an exception existed only for the royal family and the Bishop of Paris. This regulated labor practices and protected rest/observance periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and role of jurors (experienced masters as referees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every corporation had jurors who were selected among masters having at least ten years' experience, and whose business was to settle, as referees, all questions arising in business transactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced masters served as adjudicators for disputes and quality control (including material inspection). Their tenure/experience requirement served as a qualification standard for adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridge-makers' performance guarantee (payment contingent on winter test)
rubrics_metrics.description: These carpenters (bridge-makers) built at their risk, and they had no claim to payment until their work had withstood the test of the winter floods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bridges were to be tested by surviving winter floods before payment was due — a contractual quality guarantee. Bridge-makers travelled in companies and were effectively responsible for the durability of their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal examination for mastership (practical and theoretical)
rubrics_metrics.description: There the apprentice aspiring to mastership underwent the practical and theoretical examination on which his fate depended; the work executed by him on the occasion was consecrated to the patron saint of the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotion to master required passing both practical and theoretical tests administered by the brotherhood in a communal/religious setting; craftsmanship output for the exam was ceremonially dedicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of distinct trades / division of labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Bridge-makers, or 'pontiffs,' builders, joiners, ship-builders and military carpenters were recognized as distinct trades, nor could one division intrude upon the duties of the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialization was institutionalized: different branches of carpentry were separate trades with defined duties, limiting scope-creep and preserving skill standards specific to each subtrade.
